## Objectives for today

* Understand the concept and practice of partitioning the error

* Understand how to calculate variances 

## Inference 

* We want to make inferential statements about: 

   - Relationships between predictors and response

      + How big is an effect? Is an effect “important?” 

      + How certain are we about the sign and size of the effect?  

  - Prediction 

      + What do we predict for a novel case? 
      
      + How good will our predictions be? 


## Partitioning the error 

Consider a model assuming no information in our data, just random noise: 

* We call this the **model of the mean**: 

  + $y_i = \bar{y} + \epsilon_i$ 

  + OR 

  + $y_i = \beta_0 + \epsilon_i$

We can calculate our total error relative to this model: 

$$
\text{Total Error} = \epsilon_i = y_i - \bar{y}
$$


## Partitioning the error 

Now let's consider a more interesting model:

* $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i$

We know that our predictions from this model (i.e., ignoring the error) are:

* $\hat{y_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$

So let's break our total error for this model into two components: 

* The part explained by the model

* The residual error that we haven’t explained

$$
\underbrace{y_i - \bar{y}}_{\text{Total}} = \underbrace{\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}}_{\text{Model}} + \underbrace{y_i - \hat{y}_i}_{\text{Residual}}
$$


## Let's look at an example 

* Kery's wallcreeper in Switzerland 

  - $x$ = year (1990:2005)

  - $y$ = % of surveyed plots with a wallcreeper 

![](creeper.jpg){ width=50% }


## Let's look at an example 

```{r echo = FALSE, results = FALSE, fig.width = 8}

set.seed(12)

years <- 16
year <- c(1990:2005)-1989
temp <- rnorm(16,0,2)
b0 <- 30 
b1 <- -0.8
b2 <- -0.2
sigma <- 3
creepers <- b0 + b1*year + b2*temp + rnorm(years,0,sigma)

data <- data.frame(year,creepers, temp)

plot(year, creepers, main = "Percentage of surveyed plots where Kery's wallcreepers were detected, by year", ylab = "% surveyed plots", xlab = "Year")

```


## Let's fit a model to this 

Our model: 

$$percent_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1*years_i + \epsilon_i$$

Let’s find $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\; \text{and}\; \hat{\boldsymbol{y}}$

Recall:

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{y}$$

$$\mathbf{\hat{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$$

Recall also: 

$$\mathbf{\hat{y}} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{y}$$
* What do we call the quantity by which we are multiplying $\mathbf{y}$?

## Our model 

Let's do this using matrix algebra, like we learned on Monday 

* Create our design matrix, $\boldsymbol{X}$ 

```{r, echo=TRUE}
#Design matrix
years <- 16
des.mat <- t(as.matrix(rbind(rep(1,years),seq(1:years))))

``` 

## Our model 

* Have a look at our design matrix 

```{r, echo=TRUE}
#Print DM   
print(des.mat[1:10,])
```

## Our model  

* Calculate our betas  

$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{y}$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
#Calculate betas  
betas <- solve(t(des.mat)%*%des.mat)%*%t(des.mat)%*%data$creepers

``` 

## Our model  

* Calculate our predictions 

$\hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \boldsymbol{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$


```{r, echo=TRUE}
#Calculate predictions  
yhat <- des.mat%*%betas

``` 


## Think, pair, share 

What ecological hypothesis are we representing with our model 

$creepers_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1*year_i$ 

where year is c(1:16)?


## Plot the model 

$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ = `r betas[1]`,  `r betas[2]`

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8}
model.year <- lm(creepers ~ year, data = data)

yhat <- predict(model.year)

plot(year, creepers, main = "", ylab = "% surveyed plots", xlab = "Year")
lines(x = year,y=yhat)
points(x = year, y = yhat,col="blue")

```


## Partitioning the error 

```{r partition_SS, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5, fig.align="center"}
## set plot area
par(mfrow = c(1,3),
    mai = c(0.5,0.3,0.5,0.2),
    omi = c(0, 0, 0, 0),
    cex = 0.7)

## SSTO - plot y and mean(y)
plot(data$year, data$creepers, type = "n",
     bty = "l", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "")
segments(x0 = data$year, y0 = data$creepers, y1 = mean(yhat), col = "gray")
abline(h = mean(data$creepers), lty = "dashed")
points(data$year, data$creepers, pch = 19)
mtext(expression(Total: ~ italic(y[i])-bar(italic(y))), side = 3, line = 1)
mtext(expression(italic(x)), 1, line=0.2, cex=1.1, at=max(data$year))
mtext(expression(italic(y)), 2, line=0.3, cex=1.1, at=max(data$creepers), las=1)
mtext(expression(italic(bar(y))), 2, line=0.3, cex=1.1, at=mean(data$creepers), las=1)

## SSR - plot yhat and mean(yhat)
plot(data$year, data$creepers, type = "n",
     bty = "l", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "")
segments(x0 = data$year, y0 = yhat, y1 = mean(yhat), col = "gray")
points(data$year, yhat, pch = 21, bg = "white")
abline(a = coef(model.year)[1], b = coef(model.year)[2])
abline(h = mean(data$creepers), lty = "dashed")
points(data$year, yhat, pch = 21, bg = "white")
mtext(expression(Model: ~ italic(hat(y)[i])-bar(italic(y))), side = 3, line = 1)
mtext(expression(italic(x)), 1, line=0.2, cex=1.1, at=max(data$year))
mtext(expression(italic(y)), 2, line=0.3, cex=1.1, at=max(data$creepers), las=1)
mtext(expression(italic(bar(y))), 2, line=0.3, cex=1.1, at=mean(data$creepers), las=1)
mtext(expression(italic(hat(y))), 4, line=0.2, cex=1.1, at=max(data$creepers), las=1)

## SSE - plot observed and yhat
plot(data$year, data$creepers, type = "n",
     bty = "l", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "")
segments(x0 = data$year, y0 = yhat, y1 = data$creepers, col = "gray")
points(data$year, data$creepers, pch = 19)
abline(a = coef(model.year)[1], b = coef(model.year)[2])
mtext(expression(Error: ~ italic(y[i])-italic(hat(y)[i])), side = 3, line = 1)
mtext(expression(italic(x)), 1, line=0.3, cex=1.1, at=max(data$year))
mtext(expression(italic(y)), 2, line=0.3, cex=1.1, at=max(data$creepers), las=1)
mtext(expression(italic(hat(y))), 4, line=0.2, cex=1.1, at=max(data$creepers), las=1)
```


## Sum-of-squares: Total

Recall that, in least squares estimation, to calculate the overall error, we need to square the individual errors 

The total sum-of-squares $(SSTO)$ measures the total variation in the data 

$$
SSTO = \sum \left( y_i - \bar{y} \right)^2
$$


## Sum-of-squares: Model

The model (regression) sum-of-squares $(SSR)$ measures the variation between the model fits and the mean of the data

$$
SSR = \sum \left( \hat{y}_i - \bar{y} \right)^2
$$


## Sum-of-squares: Error

The error sum-of-squares $(SSE)$ measures the variation between the data and the model fits

$$
SSE = \sum \left( y_i - \hat{y}_i \right)^2
$$


## Partitioning sums-of-squares

The sums-of-squares have the same additive property as the deviations

$$
\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}_{SSTO} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2}_{SSR} + \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}_{SSE}
$$


## Our wallcreepers example

```{r, echo=TRUE}

#Run our model 
model.year <- lm(creepers ~ year, data = data)

#Get our predictions, y-hat
yhat <- matrix(predict(model.year))

#Get predictions from the model of the mean 
ybar <- matrix(predict(lm(creepers ~ 1, data = data)))

#Calculate our sums-of-squares
SSTO <- (t(data$creepers-ybar))%*%(data$creepers-ybar)

SSR <- (t(yhat-ybar))%*%(yhat-ybar)

SSE <- (t(data$creepers-yhat))%*%(data$creepers-yhat)
```


## Our wallcreepers example 

$SSTO$ = `r round(SSTO,dig=3)`

$SSR$ = `r round(SSR,dig=3)`

$SSE$ = `r round(SSE,dig=3)`


## Our wallcreepers example 

The function **anova()** will give us the sums-of-squares:

```{r, echo=TRUE}

#Compare to model output - it matches! 
anova(model.year)

```


## Goodness-of-fit

How about a measure of how well a model fits the data?

* $SSTO$ measures the variation in $y$ without considering $X$

* $SSE$ measures the reduced variation in $y$ after considering $X$

* Let's consider this reduction in variance as a proportion of the total


## Goodness-of-fit

A common option is the *coefficient of determination* or $R^2$ 

$$
R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SSTO} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SSTO} \\
~ \\
0 < R^2 < 1
$$

For our wallcreepers model 

```{r, echo = TRUE}

(r2 <- 1 - (SSE/SSTO))
```


## Goodness-of-fit


```{r, echo = TRUE}

#Check against model output - it matches! 
summary(model.year)$r.squared
```


## Degrees of freedom

The number of *independent* elements that are free to vary when estimating quantities of interest

* An example: 

   - Imagine you have 7 ponds to fish and you want to fish a new pond each day for a week.

     + On day 1 you have 7 ponds to choose from, on day 2 any of the remaining 6, and so forth

     + On day 7, you are out of choices: there is only one pond left to fish

     + You had 7 - 1 = 6 days of freedom to choose your fishing spot 


## Degrees of freedom | Linear models

Beginning with $SSTO$, we have

$$
SSTO = \sum \left( y_i - \bar{y} \right)^2
$$

The data are of dimension $n$, but estimating the mean $(\bar{y})$ from the data costs 1 degree of freedom $(df)$, so

$$
df_{SSTO} = n - 1
$$


## Degrees of freedom | Linear models

For the $SSR$ we have

$$
SSR = \sum \left( \hat{y}_i - \bar{y} \right)^2
$$

If we have $k$ parameters in our model, our parameters, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, are of dimension k, but again we lose 1 $df$ when estimating the mean, so

$$
df_{SSR} = k - 1
$$


## Degrees of freedom | Linear models

For the $SSE$

$$
SSE = \sum \left( y_i - \hat{y}_i \right)^2
$$

The data are of dimension $n$ while the predictions are of dimension $k$ so

$$
df_{SSE} = n - k
$$

Notice also that, just as we have

$SSTO = SSR + SSE$ 

we also have

$df_{SSTO} = df_{SSR} + df_{SSE} \Rightarrow (n - 1) = (k - 1) + (n - k)$

## Degrees of freedom | Linear models

Let's look at our **anova()** result again to check the df   

```{r, echo=TRUE}

anova(model.year)

```


## Mean squares

A mean square is a sum-of-squares divided by its degrees of freedom

$$
MS = \frac{SS}{df} \\
\Downarrow \\
MSR = \frac{SSR}{k - 1} ~~~ \& ~~~ MSE = \frac{SSE}{n - k} 
$$


## Variance estimates

We are typically interested in two variance estimates:

1. The variance of the residuals $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ - the unexplained variance

2. The variance of the model parameters $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ - the uncertainty in our predictions 


## Variance estimates | Residuals

In least squares estimation, we assume that the model errors (residuals) are independent and identically distributed with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2$, i.e., $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \text{N}(0,\sigma^2)$

But we don't know $\sigma^2$, we have to estimate it 


## Variance estimates | Residuals

If $z_i \sim \text{N}(0, 1)$ then

$$
\sum_{i = 1}^{n} z_i^2 = \mathbf{z}^{\top}\mathbf{z} \sim \chi^2_{n}
$$


## Variance estimates | Residuals

If $z_i \sim \text{N}(0, 1)$ then

$$
\sum_{i = 1}^{n} z_i^2 = \mathbf{z}^{\top}\mathbf{z} \sim \chi^2_{n}
$$

In our linear model, $e_i \sim \text{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ so

$$
\sum_{i = 1}^{n} e_i^2 = \mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{e} \sim \sigma^2 \cdot \chi^2_{n - k} 
$$


## Variance estimates | Residuals

Therefore, given 

$$
\mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{e} \sim \sigma^2 \cdot \chi^2_{n - k} \\
\text{E}(\chi^2_{n - k}) = n - k \\
\text{E}(\mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{e}) = SSE
$$

then

$$
SSE = \sigma^2 (n - k) ~ \Rightarrow ~ \sigma^2 = \frac{SSE}{n - k} = MSE
$$


## Our wallcreepers example 

```{r, echo = TRUE}

#Remember our calculation of error sum-of-squares
SSE <- (t(data$creepers-yhat))%*%(data$creepers-yhat)

#Get degrees of freedom and calculate MSE 
df.SSE <- length(data$creepers) - 2
  
(MSE = SSE/(df.SSE))

#Compare this to model output - it matches!  
(sigma2.year <- summary(model.year)$sigma^2)

```


## Variance estimates | Parameters

Recall that our estimate of the model parameters is 

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{y}
$$


## Variance estimates | Parameters

Estimating the variance of the model parameters $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ requires some matrix algebra

For a scalar $z$, if $\text{Var}(z) = \sigma^2$ then $\text{Var}(az) = a^2 \sigma^2$

For a vector $\mathbf{z}$, if $\text{Var}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{\Sigma}$ then $\text{Var}(\mathbf{A z}) = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{A}^{\top}$


## Variance estimates | Parameters

The variance of the parameters is therefore 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} &= (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{y} \\
   &= \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right] \mathbf{y} \\
\end{aligned} \\
\Downarrow \\
\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right] \text{Var}(\mathbf{y}) \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right]^{\top}
$$


## Variance estimates | Parameters

Recall that we can write our model in matrix form as

$$
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{\epsilon} \\
\mathbf{\epsilon} \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I})
$$


## Variance estimates | Parameters

We can rewrite our model more compactly as

$$
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{\epsilon} \\
\mathbf{\epsilon} \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}) \\
\Downarrow \\
\mathbf{y} \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}, \underbrace{\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}}_{\text{Var}(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})}) \\
$$


## Variance estimates | Parameters

Our estimate of $\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$ is then  

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) &= \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right] \text{Var}(\mathbf{y}) \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right]^{\top} \\
  &= \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right] \sigma^2 \mathbf{I} \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^{\top} \right]^{\top} \\
  &= \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X}) \left[ (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \right]^{\top} \\
  &= \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^{\top} \mathbf{X})^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$


## Our wallcreepers example 

```{r, echo = TRUE}

#calculate the variance-covariance matrix (k * k dimensions)
beta.var <- sigma2.year*solve(t(des.mat)%*%des.mat)

#the variances will be on the diagonal 
c(beta1.se <- sqrt(beta.var[1,1]), beta2.se <- sqrt(beta.var[2,2]))

#Check against our model - it matches! 
summary(model.year)$coefficients

```
